Q: How can I get the type of a polymorphic function for a specific type class instance? A:

You can use visible type application feature to specify parametric types. You can look at functions in a more creative way: Functions in Haskell can be applied to not only values of some types, but also to types of those values. But to pass a type, you should somehow specify (with prepending @) that you're passing types (because types are not first-class objects in Haskell yet).

So here is how it works:

λ: :set -XTypeApplications
λ: :t ap @((->) Int)
ap @((->) Int) :: (Int -> a -> b) -> (Int -> a) -> Int -> b

The only limitation of such an approach is that you can't use type variables in GHCi. You should use specific types (Int instead of r), but this is not a big deal.

ADVANCED SECTION

Well, actually you can, but it's tricky:

λ: :set -XExplicitForAll
λ: :set -XPartialTypeSignatures
λ: :set -XScopedTypeVariables
λ: :{
λ| foo :: forall r . _
λ| foo = ap @((->) r)
λ| :}
<interactive>:28:19: warning: [-Wpartial-type-signatures]
    • Found type wildcard ‘_’
        standing for ‘(r -> a -> b) -> (r -> a) -> r -> b’
λ: :t foo
foo :: (r -> a -> b) -> (r -> a) -> r -> b

You can actually use placeholders instead of type variables (see another answer). But if you want to specify the exact names, use the approach from above.

λ: :t ap @((->) _)
ap @((->) _) :: (t -> a -> b) -> (t -> a) -> t -> b

/ADVANCED SECTION

One more thing to say about this approach: you should do something more if your functions have several type parameters and you want to specify the exact one. Types are passed one by one from left to right, just as simple arguments in some function like bar :: Int -> String -> Double.

If you want to fix the first argument of bar, you should write bar 5, and if you want to fix the second, then, well, you can write something like \n -> bar n "baz", but this doesn't work with a type application. You need to know two things:

  1. The order of types.
  2. How to specify the desired type.

Consider the following function:

λ: :t lift
lift :: (Monad m, MonadTrans t) => m a -> t m a

We want be able to specify the m and t type variables. Because Haskell doesn’t have any named type variables (yet), you can't write :t lift {t=MaybeT} or :t lift {m=IO} unfortunately. So go back to two things.

To see the order of types, you should use some compiler options. The order of type arguments is specified by forall, and you can do it manually. Otherwise, type parameters will be sorted somehow by the compiler. Mere mortals can't see the order of types for the lift function, but if you're aware of some high-level magic you can:

λ: :set -fprint-explicit-foralls
λ: :t lift
lift
  :: forall {t :: (* -> *) -> * -> *} {a} {m :: * -> *}.
     (Monad m, MonadTrans t) =>
     m a -> t m a

And then you should use @_ to skip some types:

λ: :t lift @MaybeT
lift @MaybeT
  :: forall {a} {m :: * -> *}. Monad m => m a -> MaybeT m a
λ: :t lift @_ @IO
lift @_ @IO
  :: forall {t :: (* -> *) -> * -> *} {a}.
     MonadTrans t =>
     IO a -> t IO a
λ: :t lift @_ @_ @Int
lift @_ @_ @Int
  :: forall {t :: (* -> *) -> * -> *} {t1 :: * -> *}.
     (Monad t1, MonadTrans t) =>
     t1 Int -> t t1 Int

Well, this is really a mystery for me why m is shown as the third argument in forall, but it should be passed as the second, but I'm still not aware of all magic.

Q: What is best, React or Flutter? A:

You're right; by "native" I meant "OS-platform native", using "real" platform-provided widgets - I didn't mean in the sense of native machine-code vs. JavaScript/WASM.

In that same sense I wrote "full advantage of the platform", pointing not to CPU hardware features, but OS platform features: for example, when you use React in a stock Safari WebView then you can't access the iPhone's depth-sensing camera at all. Things like that.

Q: Tamper Proof Excel Document using java A:

While this might be too late for the original question, I’d like to leave this here for future reference.

I would recommend UVerify, not only for Excel files but for data integrity use cases in general. It also provides a Java SDK.

implementation 'io.uverify:uverify-sdk:0.1.5'

Certification and verification would look like this:

UVerifyClient client = UVerifyClient.builder()
    .signMessage(message -> wallet.signData(address, message))
    .signTx(unsignedTx -> wallet.signTx(unsignedTx))
    .build();

// create
client.issueCertificates(
    "addr1...",
    List.of(new CertificateData("sha256-hash-of-document", "SHA-256", "")))

// verify
List<CertificateResponse> certs = client.verify("sha256-or-sha512-hex-hash");

A full end-to-end examples are available here: https://github.com/UVerify-io/uverify-examples/tree/main/java

It anchors the file hash on the Cardano blockchain, ensuring that nobody, not even the person who created the file, can change it and simply sign it again with an old timestamp.

You can send the deep link together with your certificate: https://uverify.io/verify/<file_hash>

For example, if you issue a laboratory report and do not store any data, you can simply send the file to the patient without any link. If the patient brings the report back to your platform years later, you can hash the file and check whether https://uverify.io/verify/<file_hash> returns a certificate created by your laboratory at the relevant point in time. You can then safely continue processing the file, knowing that it has not been tampered with.

Since creating a blockchain entry comes with a gas fee, currently around €0.07 per hash, you might also want to look into data structures like Merkle trees. They allow you to periodically put a proof for thousands of documents on chain by anchoring only a single hash.

If you want to maintain versions, Merkle Patricia Tries are probably what you are looking for.

This might be overkill for many use cases, but if data integrity from a specific point in time matters, it is a viable approach without relying on a centralized third party.

Q: Difference between User and System Installer of Visual Studio Code A:

The good old PoLP... Visual Studio Code is from a trusted publisher but extensions that are installed can come from 3rd parties and aren't guaranteed to be trustworthy so running them as admin (SYSTEM user) could be even more +catastrophic if you mess up (we all do). I'll give a couple scenarios where your choice would be something worth considering:

Per-user install:

You're at home, you're the only person who logs into your machine and your user has admin rights already... No real need for installing as SYSTEM user/admin and its a smarter choice just in case.

or maybe

You're at a business where you don't manage their IT systems, your PC might be shared with others, or you don't have admin permissions given by your company but still have basic permissions to work with...

System install

Let's say you're at home, have multiple accounts that you use (for different aliases/other purposes) you might not want to download the same extensions or tools again on each account.... Or speculation, you might have a small company with no DC (domain controller) or serious business IT infrastructure.... You might have a small team that you want the same tools available to them when you/they log into the PC....

or maybe

You're in a large company, but many users share a machine. Or lets say, you have private tools/extensions (for anything, not just VS Code) and installing system-wide makes much more sense to save an individual user having a misconfiguration of their software - which might or might not cause big problems when what they produce turns out different to what the company expects....

------------------------------------------------------------

I doubt I've given a definitive answer on the "best" option, because what's best for me isn't necessarily the best option for you. Hope I've given you or other readers a bit of insight at least

P.S. Thanks @dbc moderator for editing the profanities out of my answer. Used to reading here, not commenting.. Took a few attempts just to get it formatting right. - appreciate it mate!

Q: Finding the longest two words per input text file A:

You can also use the built-in features bash provides to isolate each word in each input file and obtain its length without spawning additional subshells for strings, etc. The following simply

  • loops over each filename provided as a command-line parameter,
  • validates the filename is a file that exists and is non-empty,
  • loops reading each line and mapping each word into the array words,
  • loops over each word outputting the length and word analyzed.

This doesn't contain any logic to preserve or compare the length to determine the longest, but that is left to you. As @Lea Gris points out you can map the entire file, and that can be more efficient provided the files are not large. For megabytes of data, the line-at-a-time can save the allocation overhead at the expense of an additional loop over the lines.

A short example of these operations could be:

#!/bin/bash

for f in "$@"; do                         # loop over files
  [ -s "$f" ] || continue                 # exists and non-empty
  printf '\n%s\n\n' "$f"                  # output filename
  while read -r line; do                  # read line
    mapfile -t words <<< "$line"          # words array from line
    for w in ${words[@]}; do              # loop each word
      printf '%2d - %s\n' "${#w}" "$w"    # output length and word
    done
  done < "$f"                             # feed line loop from file
done

Slight Modification with pipe to sort and tail for two longest words

While you can limit the internals to bash builtins, it may make sense to pipe the output to ready made shell tools to capture the two-longest (or however many longest) words you like by piping to sort and tail. The impact on efficiency is mitigated as no subshell is called within a loop. For instance you can grab the longest two words (with increasing alphabetical sort if the longest words have different spellings but the same length) with something like the following:

#!/bin/bash

{
for f in "$@"; do                         # loop over files
  [ -s "$f" ] || continue                 # exists and non-empty
  while read -r line; do                  # read line
    mapfile -t words <<< "$line"          # words array from line
    for w in ${words[@]}; do              # loop each word
      printf '%2d %s\n' "${#w}" "$w"      # output length and word
    done
  done < "$f"                             # feed line loop from file
done
} | sort -u -k1n -k2 | tail -n2

Something to consider. You can adjust how many words with the options to tail and you can come up with a way to handle multiple words all having the same length to your liking.

No one way is "better" than the other, so consider them all. If dealing with large files, then look at the efficiencies and tailor your script to your data.
